node.label: Alice Clark
node.description: Studies women’s paid and unpaid production through overlapping household and capitalist arrangements. Differences of class and marital position shape her account of changing work, training and authority; her chronology and assumptions about earlier households remain contested.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919). Compare with Pinchbeck’s later-period study to examine how historians explain the relationship between economic change and women’s autonomy.
node.scope_note: The 1919 preface credits Schreiner, Knowles and Power’s unpublished research. Introduction and conclusion distinguish production for use, family enterprise and individual wages, while admitting conjectural medieval comparisons and incomplete causal evidence. Maternal and racial assumptions belong to Clark’s historical position. Erickson’s 1992 introduction values unpaid-work analysis while disputing chronology and household equality. Main occupational cases are not newly read; neither timeless equality nor a uniform decline for all women is established.

named_group_routes.relationship: Staples history as a disputed Canadian antecedent of environmental history: Cook's continuity claim (1990) and Forkey's rejection (1998)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period texts first; they disagree. (1) Continuity: Ramsay Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) claims a long Canadian concern with environment: 'In a broad sense the writing of Canadian history has always been concerned with the environment' (p. 6). Against reading the older historians as nationalists only, he writes that nationalism 'was not a full-time interest for any of them. Certainly not Harold Innis for whom the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staple products were the real stuff of history' (p. 6). He also marks a break: 'Innis, Lower and Creighton also struggled with the question of the impact of the North American environment on European women and men', but 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), and 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus' (p. 7). (2) Rejection: Neil Forkey (CHR 79:1, 1998) rejects the line: 'Although the environment was an ingredient in the work of Harold A. Innis, Donald Creighton, and Arthur R.M. Lower, their studies do not serve as prototypes for Canadian environmental history'; 'In their approach, the environment exists only as a scaffolding on which human history unfolds, and not as an actor in the process' (p. 70). 'The staples model masks the essential role of social relationships and the dynamic between humans and nature', and 'More appropriate antecedents' are found in the historical geographer Andrew H. Clark (p. 71; n. 6 cites The Fur Trade in Canada and The Cod Fisheries). Classification: 'influence' here records a proposed antecedent that Canadian environmental historians disputed, not an established transmission of method; no in-period text read shows environmental historians taking up staples method, and neither position is presented as the Canadian field's. Later readings (2003–2024), labelled as such and not the evidence this edge rests on: Graeme Wynn (2003 review, p. 96) agrees that Forkey is right 'to puncture' claims 'that the staples approach represents an indigenous form of proto-environmental history'; Wynn (2004, p. 33) writes that the staples works 'focused on human uses of the environment', with 'little concern in this work for the reciprocity and mutuality of relations between people and nature'. Tina Loo (2014, p. 622) reclaims the work: 'it could be argued that some of the most influential work on the country's past was a kind of global environmental history, even if its practitioners did not call it that', naming Innis and Lower. Daniel Macfarlane's entry in NiCHE's 'Crash Course in Canadian Environmental History' (2024) holds that Innis's legacy 'still shapes many key debates and approaches in contemporary Canadian environmental history' and that, through works such as Cronon's Nature's Metropolis, the staples and metropolitan-hinterland theses 'are perhaps Canada's biggest contribution to international environmental history'. The edge records a proposed antecedent the field disagreed over; it does not say that Innis wrote environmental history or founded the field. Innis's books are unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Metropolitanism: Canadian history read through metropolitan centres that organize frontiers and hinterlands, proposed as a wider framework than the frontier-environmentalist reading (1954)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History', Canadian Historical Review 35:1 (1954), pp. 1–21, read in full in an Internet Archive scan of the issue. He sorts English-Canadian historiography into 'schools', 'merely for convenience' (p. 2): a Britannic school, a School of Political Nationhood, and 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All', which 'built particularly on the concept of the frontier in North American history derived from Turner' (p. 5); he names Munro, Underhill, Sage, Lower, Landon, A. S. Morton and A. L. Burt, adding that 'no tight determinism is intended in thus naming these authors, nor, on the whole, did they display any' (p. 6, n. 6). He finds in them 'a certain tendency to fix values', so that western farmers were 'Good' and eastern business men 'Evil' (p. 12), and 'a tendency to overvalue the influence of native North American forces and the material environment, and a tendency to undervalue forces transferred from Europe and the non-material environment' (pp. 13–14); 'while in no way underrating the very great contributions which frontierism and environmentalism have made', it 'does seem necessary to look for a wider framework' (p. 14). The Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton offered 'a metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint', and 'The result was virtually to establish “metropolitanism” in Canadian historiography' (p. 16). The metropolis is 'a city of outstanding size' dominating 'other cities and their countrysides, the whole area being organized by the metropolis, through control of communications, trade, and finance, into one economic and social unit' (p. 17), in 'almost a feudal chain of vassalage' (p. 17); 'the rise of metropolitanism is the other side of the coin to frontier expansion' (p. 18). His examples include the Clear Grits organized around Toronto, the Globe and George Brown (p. 19). He limits the claim: 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism' (p. 19), and concedes that a metropolitan interpretation may 'only restate old problems in somewhat different terms. It may be so: but what is particularly needed is a restatement' (p. 21). A contribution, not a founding: he credits Lower's Colony to Nation and essays, Masters's The Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31), and the Laurentian school (p. 16). In-period reception and criticism, from Donald F. Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), pp. 95–113, read in full: the article 'heralded the arrival of “metropolitanism” as a “vitalizing approach”'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); for most historians it became, in Carl Berger's words as Davis quotes them, 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96). Davis quotes W. L. Morton's objection that the metropolitan thesis, 'which he associated with both Creighton and Careless', 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (p. 98), and S. D. Clark's at the 1974 CHA meeting that 'it serves no useful purpose to work with such categories or concepts as metropolis and hinterland when what is metropolis can also be considered hinterland' (p. 107); both are quoted-in witnesses, not read here. Davis's own judgment: Careless, combining Gras's ecological model with the Laurentian school's elites, 'has produced a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research' (p. 102); his interpretation 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'the Gras-Careless statement of metropolitanism is weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103). Davis also reports that Careless disclaimed 'such a metropolitan “thesis”' in 1973 while keeping the 'approach' (p. 96, quoting Acadiensis 3, 1973). edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition) stays: it records the urban historians' critique at group level.

named_group_routes.relationship: Coal in explanations of British industrialisation, as readers compare them: Mokyr places Pomeranz in a tradition “established by … E.A. Wrigley” (2002); Huang says Pomeranz simplified “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument” (2002); Clark and Jacks find that both “have made coal central to the story” (2007)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Readers’ comparisons, read. Mokyr (October 2002 draft, p. 2): Pomeranz’s coal argument “joins a venerable tradition established by Carlo Cipolla, E.A. Wrigley and others that looks at the Industrial Revolution as primarily a revolution of fossil fuel usage”. Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 532–533, read in revision 1.144): Wrigley (1988) is “a very different thing from arguing that chance, or coal, alone mattered”; Pomeranz has turned “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument that chance figured in England’s industrialization into a simple argument that coal and colonies alone mattered.” Clark and Jacks (European Review of Economic History 2007, abstract): “both E. A. Wrigley and Kenneth Pomeranz have made coal central to the story”; their coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England’s possession of coal reserves. A comparison, not an influence: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read (the read pages of The Great Divergence cite Wrigley only on England’s early divergence from the continent, p. 6 n. 8). Wrigley’s argument stresses chance and the end of the organic economy; Pomeranz pairs coal with colonies.

sources.title: J. M. S. Careless, "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History," Canadian Historical Review 35, no. 1 (1954): 1–21.
sources.citation: J. M. S. Careless, "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History," Canadian Historical Review 35, no. 1 (1954): 1–21.

verification.note: Article unread; no abstract available. The metropolitan argument is described here only at title level and through Davis 1985's account of metropolitan theses. Checked against: Crossref DOI record (CHR 35:1, March 1954, pp. 1–21); reprints in One West, Two Myths II (University of Calgary Press, 2007) via Crossref; OpenAlex description of Careless at Work (selected essays) names frontierism and metropolitanism as a main preoccupation. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full (pp. 1–21) for the 1.135 person entry in the Internet Archive scan of the issue (sim_canadian-historical-review_1954-03_35_1; OCR checked against the page image for p. 16). The earlier description through Davis is superseded. Quoted: 'frontierism' named 'for want of a more precise term' and the frontier thesis 'proper' never adopted 'as fully or dogmatically in Canada' (p. 1); schools 'merely for convenience' (p. 2); 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All' (p. 5); its members and 'no tight determinism is intended' (p. 6, n. 6); Turner's 'open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6); 'environmental determinism at its most forthright' and the defenders of Turner (p. 7); 'a certain tendency to fix values' (p. 12); overvaluing native and material forces (pp. 13–14); 'a wider framework' (p. 14); the Laurentian 'metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint' and 'virtually to establish “metropolitanism”' (p. 16); the metropolis defined and the 'feudal chain of vassalage', Masters and Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31); 'the other side of the coin to frontier expansion', 'thus is Turner answered', the frontier 'a dependent' (p. 18); 'a metropolitan determinism' and the Clear Grits, Toronto and the Globe (p. 19); frontierism 'borrowed from the United States' (p. 20); 'restates old problems', 'has had its use and its day' (p. 21). Davis (1985) cites the 1967 reprint in Approaches to Canadian History, pp. 78–79.

sources.citation: Donald F. Davis, "The 'Metropolitan Thesis' and the Writing of Canadian Urban History," Urban History Review 14, no. 2 (1985): 95–113.

verification.note: Abstract read: there is no single metropolitan thesis but several approaches; urban historians would do better to abandon the metropolitan approach for its indeterminacy about relations between classes. Checked against: Crossref DOI record with French abstract (Érudit). Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full (pp. 95–113, text and notes) for the 1.135 person entry, in the Érudit PDF. Quoted: 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); Berger's 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96; n. 1 cites Berger in Canada Since 1867, 1977, pp. 87–88); metropolitanism and 'the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history'; Artibise and Linteau (1984): 'the self-conscious beginning of urban history'; Careless 'the godfather of their subdiscipline'; Stelter (1977): 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history'; Careless (1973): 'I would disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96); five approaches, Careless's the 'ecological'; Lower 'some eight years before' (p. 97); W. L. Morton's objection, quoted from 'Canada's History and Historians' (p. 98, n. 19); Careless's own account of his debt to Gras, from a letter of 11 July 1983 (p. 101, nn. 47, 51); 'a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness', 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'fallen into desuetude', Artibise's 'not really a theory', 'weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103); S. D. Clark at the 1974 CHA meeting (p. 107); Careless on Turner on television (p. 109). The 'near-doctrinal status' remark (p. 96) is from a private letter (n. 2) and is not used. [creighton draft: Read in full for the 1.135 Creighton entry (Érudit PDF via the Internet Archive capture of 26 September 2024; UHR 14:2, October 1985, pp. 95–113). Careless's 1954 article 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (p. 95); Harrison (1981, p. 25) quoted: Creighton 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1980 reprint, p. 107) quoted: Creighton emphasized 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played'; Morton ('Canada's History and Historians', reprint pp. 34–35) quoted: the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (pp. 97–98); Careless said he drew 'neither from Creighton or Innis' but from medieval social history and N. S. B. Gras, and melded Gras with 'the Laurentian School, then regnant' (p. 101). Morton's texts themselves are unread.] Addendum 2026-10-26: Fresh complete official Érudit PDF obtained; selected printed 96 and 109/n3 plus Artibise/Linteau-specific concluding passage read, not entire article reread. Davis quotes their 1984 Report 4 p6 acknowledgment of Careless’s contribution, coauthorship intact. He separately endorses their complaint about missing immediate-hinterland/suburban studies. Their report’s full PDF remains inaccessible, but selected own printed 6 indexed text was freshly read. Davis himself has no graph person endpoint; David Brion Davis/Natalie Zemon Davis are different people.

Addendum 2026-10-18: Revision 1.144: the whole article was OCRed (tesseract) from the same JSTOR scan; pp. 501–503, 511–512, 515 and 530–535 read closely, the rest searched. p. 501 thanks "Chris Isett … Robert Brenner"; p. 502: "It is not built on original research, but rather relies on past secondary scholarship"; p. 503: "what I termed in my work development (involving increased labor productivity), to distinguish it from involution (involving diminishing marginal returns per unit of labor) and intensification (added labor input per unit of land) in the Yangzi delta (1990, 11)"; p. 512: "growth (in output) without development (in labor productivity) … the familization of production"; p. 515 cites Geertz 1963 (pp. 130–43) only for Japan; pp. 530–531 tie his Qing law studies ("a survival ethic") to the argument; p. 533: Pomeranz's coal argument "places the cart before the horse", and "Pomeranz, I wish to emphasize, has made a useful contribution"; p. 534: England and the delta "were in fact virtually at opposite poles in a continuum from development to involution". The second research pass (evidence-pomeranz.pass2.md §2) OCRed the same scan (all 38 article pages, 200 dpi) and read pp. 501–503, 514–515, 520–521 and 532–534 in full, p. 508 (n. 7) and the reference list pp. 536–538; pp. 520–521: Pomeranz "tries to take the revolution out of de Vries' industrious revolution", and Huang (p. 521) "ignores … the evidence de Vries and others have generated to document the big changes in consumption patterns", as that pass reads it. Quoted: 'In a broad sense the writing of Canadian history has always been concerned with the environment' (p. 6); nationalism 'was not a full-time interest for any of them. Certainly not Harold Innis for whom the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staple products were the real stuff of history' (p. 6); 'Innis, Lower and Creighton also struggled with the question of the impact of the North American environment on European women and men' (p. 6); 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7); 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus' (p. 7). Note 4 cites Richard White, PHR 1985. Crossref 10.3138/jcs.25.4.5. [Also checked under pe131_crosby_cook_1990: Project MUSE PDF (University of Saskatchewan access, downloaded 2026-10-13 for the canon evidence file) re-read at p. 13 and note 35. Crossref 10.3138/jcs.25.4.5: JCS 25(4), issued January 1991, 5–16. 'Contact between Europe and North America, then, must be understood in the widest possible terms'; 'As Alfred W. Crosbie [sic], Jr., demonstrated so brilliantly nearly two decades ago, in his Columbian Exchange The Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492, contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments. Biological exchange in the form of pathogens that caused epidemic disease in populations where no immunity existed was perhaps the most spectacularly devastating consequence of contact. But the exchange of plants and animals was no less significant' (p. 13). Note 35 cites The Columbian Exchange (Greenwood, 1972) and Larocque (1982) on European diseases among Indigenous peoples in Quebec.] [Also checked under pe131_richard_white_cook_1990: Project MUSE PDF (downloaded 2026-10-13 for canon-evidence-canada.md; re-read at p. 6 and the notes). p. 6: earlier Canadian historians wrote about the environment, as in the United States 'where, as Morton knew, F.J. Note 22 also cites White, 'Native Americans and the Environment', in W. R. Swagerty, ed., Scholars and the Indian Experience (1989), 179–201.]

verification.note: Expanded primary introduction check in the same later-edition preview: opening 3–4; regional-unit discussion from 7 through comparison section 10; chapter 2 household paragraph 17/note 27; chapter 6 overview from 20 through geographical-coverage conclusion 27. Intervening passages and main chapters unread; selected passages, not full introduction. Explicit resources: Wong 1997, Tilly 1984 and Mokyr 1976; Huang 1990 is a named disagreement. Quantitative historical claims not independently tested. This source remains the 2000 book, not the later 2002 exchange. Tilly title/date corroborated by publisher-supplied BiblioVault record 9780871548795; Mokyr 1976 title corroborated by journal bibliographic record. Those original books were not newly read. Addendum 2026-10-13: Whole introduction pp. 3–27 re-read in the later-edition preview (pagination of that edition), with contents pp. v–vii and index pages. Quoted for the 1.130 person entry: 'The book thus calls upon the fruits of overseas coercion to help explain the difference between European development and what we see in certain other parts of Eurasia (primarily China and Japan)—not the whole of that development'; 'Thus the book combines comparative analysis, some purely local contingency, and an integrative or global approach'; 'we have, instead, a polycentric world with no dominant center' (p. 4). 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong' (p. 7). 'truly reciprocal'; 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed'; 'viewing both sides of the comparison as “deviations” when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm'; n. 13: 'much more about some he does not treat extensively, such as environmental change' (p. 8). 'comparison and the analysis of connections become indistinguishable' (p. 10). Chapter 5 'offers a systematic comparison of ecological constraints in selected key areas of China and Europe'; Europe 'rescued by a combination of overseas resources and England’s breakthrough (partly conditioned by geographic good luck) in the use of subterranean stores of energy'; parallels with Sugihara Kaoru (p. 12). 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?'; 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' (p. 19). Shortages 'of fuel and building materials' in all the densest cores (p. 20). 'what was truly scarce: land and energy'; 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). 'We end, then, with connections and interactions explaining what comparison alone cannot'; 'joining the burgeoning field of “world history,”'; 'adding a few Chinese and Japanese foils to a European story does not make it “world history.”' (p. 25). Contents: Part Three 'Beyond Smith and Malthus: From Ecological Constraints to Sustained Industrial Growth'; chapter 5 'Shared Constraints: Ecological Strain in Western Europe and East Asia' (211); chapter 6 'Abolishing the Land Constraint: The Americas as a New Kind of Periphery' (264). Chapters 1–6 and the appendices are unread; quantitative claims are not tested. verification.note: Scanned pages 1059–60 checked for Marxist feminist approaches, British socialist-feminist debates, and Scott’s criticism of economic determination. This is her intervention, not a consensus account of all gender history. Additional primary pp. 1067–1068 checked in revision 1.25: Rosaldo and Foucault named, gender defined relationally, institutions and subjective identity distinguished, and universal psychoanalytic claims qualified. Full article remains unreviewed. Additional 2026-09-12 reading: complete printed pp. 1062–1066 through OCR of PDF indices 10–14. Scott finds constructed subjectivity instructive but criticizes universal binary antagonism and insufficient historical variability; she discusses Sally Alexander, de Lauretis and Riley and productively cites Derrida. Davis’s words are as Scott quotes them.
